newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Interconnector to weigh on European gas prices.
newsitem.headline: Interconnector to weigh on European gas prices.

text.p: The Britain-Belgium Interconnector gas pipeline will cut European gas prices and boost competition between producers when it comes on stream in October 1998, one of the consortium's partners said on Friday.
"In England prices can rise somewhat but they should fall slightly on the continent," said John Vermeire, commercial director of Belgian natural gas distributor Distrigaz.
"It will also increase competition between gas producers," he told a news conference.

The 450 million pounds ($675 million) Interconnector, the first gas pipeline to link Britain with continental Europe, will be able to carry up to 20 billion cubic metres of natural gas a year from Britain's Bacton, Norfolk, terminal to Zeebrugge.
About 8.5 billion cubic metres a year will flow in the opposite direction.

Interconnector managing director Roger Cornish said two sales contracts have already been announced -- by British Gas Plc and by DuPont's Conoco -- accounting for three of the 20 billion cubic metres.
"But...other shippers are currently in the market to sell capacity," he said.
He ruled out potential financial woes for the Interconnector as the gas shippers which purchased capacity on the pipeline would pay regardless of whether gas came through it or not.
"Shareholdes are ensured of revenue, that's why it is better to be shareholder of Interconnector than shareholder of Eurotunnel," said Vermeire.
Vermeire said the Interconnector would boost Belgium's importance as a gas transit country with the annual flow of 13 billion expected to double by the year 2000.
"It will have major advantages for Belgium -- improve infrastructure, ensure supplies and improve its buying position," he said.

Vermeire said Belgium had been preferred over the Netherlands, Germany and France mainly because it was not a gas producer itself which ruled out any conflicts of interest, and already had a considerable gas infrastructure.
Construction work started in Zeebrugge on October 14 and will begin in Bacton at the end of this month.
Of the 235 kms 40-inch pipeline, less than five kms are on land, said Dirk Deberdt, Interconnector Onshore manager Belgium.

He said the onland work had to be completed by mid-June -- before the start of the 1997 summer holiday season. Construction of the gas terminals in Zeebrugge and Bacton is due to finish at the end of May 1997.
Works at sea will begin around New Year, said project manager Peter Devinck.
He said about 210 kms of pipelines would have to be laid on the bottom of the North Sea, which had to be levelled.

The long Belgian beach at Zeebrugge was another major problem with about 500 metres of pipes to be dragged underneath the beach, dunes, a nature reserve including protected sweetwater ponds and a key coastal road.
Partners in the Interconnector consortium are British Gas, Conoco, British Petroleum, Elf Aquitaine, Gazprom, Distrigaz, Ruhrgas, Amerada Hess and National Power.
